problems.unit: Vector spaces, subspaces, sums, and direct sums
problems.title: The zero vector really is neutral
problems.objective: Verify the additive identity coordinate by coordinate in a concrete vector space.
problems.statement: Let $v=(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$. Prove that $(0,0)+v=v$ and $v+(0,0)=v$ using coordinatewise addition.
permittedResults: Equality in $\mathbb R^2$ is coordinatewise.
The real number $0$ is the additive identity.
problems.strategy: First: Write out both coordinatewise sums. Next: Simplify $0+x$ and $x+0$ in each coordinate. Finally: Use equality of ordered pairs to close both identities.
hints: Write out both coordinatewise sums.
Simplify $0+x$ and $x+0$ in each coordinate.
Use equality of ordered pairs to close both identities.
problems.solution: Coordinatewise addition gives $(0,0)+(x,y)=(0+x,0+y)=(x,y)$ and $(x,y)+(0,0)=(x+0,y+0)=(x,y)$. Thus $(0,0)$ is a two-sided additive identity.
rubricCriteria: Expands both requested sums coordinatewise.
Uses the scalar zero identities in both coordinates.
Concludes both left and right vector identities.

commonErrors.description: Claims that the neutral vector is $(1,1)$ because $1$ is neutral for multiplication.
commonErrors.consequence: Vector addition uses the scalar additive identity, so $(1,1)+(x,y)$ is generally not $(x,y)$.

commonErrors.description: Checks only left addition by the zero vector.
commonErrors.consequence: The problem explicitly requests both coordinatewise identities.

problems.flawedProof: The neutral vector is $(1,1)$ because multiplying either coordinate by $1$ leaves it unchanged. Hence $(1,1)+v=v$ on both sides.

    (0 : ℝ × ℝ) + v = v ∧ v + (0 : ℝ × ℝ) = v := by

problems.unit: Vector spaces, subspaces, sums, and direct sums
problems.title: Scalar zero annihilates every vector
problems.objective: Calculate scalar multiplication by zero without appealing to geometric intuition.
problems.statement: For $v=(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$, prove that $0v=(0,0)$.
permittedResults: Scalar multiplication in $\mathbb R^2$ is coordinatewise.
$0x=0$ for every real $x$.
problems.strategy: First: Replace $0v$ by $0(x,y)$. Next: Distribute the scalar into the two coordinates. Finally: Simplify both scalar products to zero.
hints: Replace $0v$ by $0(x,y)$.
Distribute the scalar into the two coordinates.
Simplify both scalar products to zero.
problems.solution: For $v=(x,y)$, scalar multiplication is defined coordinatewise, so $0v=0(x,y)=(0x,0y)$. Since $0x=0$ and $0y=0$ in $\mathbb R$, this equals $(0,0)$, the zero vector of $\mathbb R^2$.
rubricCriteria: Uses the coordinate definition of scalar multiplication.
Simplifies both coordinates correctly.
Identifies the result as the zero vector.

commonErrors.description: Treats $0v$ as the original vector because zero is an identity.
commonErrors.consequence: Zero is the additive identity, not the multiplicative identity for scalar multiplication.

commonErrors.description: Shows only that the first coordinate vanishes.
commonErrors.consequence: Equality of vectors requires both coordinates.

problems.flawedProof: Since $0$ is the identity element of the real numbers, multiplying $v$ by $0$ leaves $v$ unchanged. Therefore $0v=v$.

Compute the second coordinate of $u+v$.
Compute the second coordinate of $cu$ and show both are zero.

Verifies additive closure by a coordinate computation.

commonErrors.consequence: Containing zero alone does not prove closure under addition and scalar multiplication.

problems.unit: Vector spaces, subspaces, sums, and direct sums
problems.title: Two coordinate axes meet only at zero
problems.objective: Determine an intersection from simultaneous coordinate conditions.
problems.statement: Let $H=\{(x,0):x\in\mathbb R\}$ and $V=\{(0,y):y\in\mathbb R\}$. Prove that $H\cap V=\{(0,0)\}$.
permittedResults: Two ordered pairs are equal exactly when their coordinates agree.
Set equality may be proved by two inclusions.
problems.strategy: First: Take a vector in both $H$ and $V$. Next: Its second coordinate is zero from $H$, and its first coordinate is zero from $V$. Finally: Check conversely that $(0,0)$ belongs to both axes.
hints: Take a vector in both $H$ and $V$.
Its second coordinate is zero from $H$, and its first coordinate is zero from $V$.
Check conversely that $(0,0)$ belongs to both axes.
problems.solution: If $(a,b)\in H\cap V$, membership in $H$ gives $b=0$ and membership in $V$ gives $a=0$, so $(a,b)=(0,0)$. Conversely, $(0,0)$ lies in both $H$ and $V$. Therefore the intersection is exactly $\{(0,0)\}$.
rubricCriteria: Uses both membership conditions for a vector in the intersection.
Derives that both coordinates vanish.
Proves the reverse inclusion by checking the zero vector.

commonErrors.consequence: Both axes contain the origin, so their intersection is not empty.

commonErrors.consequence: That proves only one inclusion of the requested equality.

problems.title: The diagonal is closed under vector operations
problems.objective: Prove that equality of coordinates is preserved by addition and scaling.
problems.statement: Let $D=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x=y\}$. Prove that if $u,v\in D$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, then $u+v\in D$ and $cu\in D$.
permittedResults: Membership in $D$ is the equality of the two coordinates.
Equality is preserved by addition and multiplication.
problems.strategy: First: Write the two coordinate equalities supplied by $u,v\in D$. Next: Add those equalities to compare the coordinates of $u+v$. Finally: Multiply the equality for $u$ by $c$ to compare the coordinates of $cu$.
hints: Write the two coordinate equalities supplied by $u,v\in D$.
Add those equalities to compare the coordinates of $u+v$.
Multiply the equality for $u$ by $c$ to compare the coordinates of $cu$.
problems.solution: From $u\in D$ and $v\in D$ we have $u_1=u_2$ and $v_1=v_2$. Hence $u_1+v_1=u_2+v_2$, so $u+v\in D$. Also $cu_1=cu_2$, so $cu\in D$.
rubricCriteria: States the coordinate equalities encoded by diagonal membership.
Proves additive closure from those equalities.
Proves scalar closure for an arbitrary scalar.

commonErrors.description: Assumes that every line in the plane is automatically a subspace.
commonErrors.consequence: Affine lines not through the origin are not subspaces, so the closure argument must be supplied.

commonErrors.description: Checks only addition and not scalar multiplication.
commonErrors.consequence: Both closure properties are requested.

problems.flawedProof: The set $D$ is a line, and every line in $\mathbb R^2$ is a vector subspace. Therefore it is closed under both operations.

problems.unit: Vector spaces, subspaces, sums, and direct sums
problems.title: A homogeneous equation defines a subspace
problems.objective: Verify closure for the solution set of one homogeneous linear equation.
problems.statement: Let $S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x+2y=0\}$. Prove that $S$ is closed under vector addition and real scalar multiplication.
permittedResults: Real addition and multiplication distribute.
A subset containing zero and closed under addition and scaling is a subspace.
problems.strategy: First: Let $u,v$ satisfy the defining equation. Next: Add their equations to test $u+v$. Finally: Multiply the equation for $u$ by an arbitrary scalar to test $cu$.
hints: Let $u,v$ satisfy the defining equation.
Add their equations to test $u+v$.
Multiply the equation for $u$ by an arbitrary scalar to test $cu$.
problems.solution: If $u_1+2u_2=0$ and $v_1+2v_2=0$, then $(u_1+v_1)+2(u_2+v_2)=(u_1+2u_2)+(v_1+2v_2)=0$. For $c\in\mathbb R$, $cu_1+2cu_2=c(u_1+2u_2)=0$. Thus $S$ is closed under both operations; it also contains $(0,0)$, so it is a subspace.
rubricCriteria: Uses arbitrary vectors satisfying the homogeneous equation.
Derives the defining equation for their sum.
Derives the defining equation after arbitrary scalar multiplication.

commonErrors.description: Treats $x+2y=0$ as two separate equations $x=0$ and $y=0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The solution set is a line with nonzero vectors, not only the origin.

commonErrors.description: Uses one numerical pair instead of arbitrary members of the set.
commonErrors.consequence: A sample calculation cannot prove universal closure.

problems.flawedProof: From $x+2y=0$ we must have $x=0$ and $y=0$. Thus $S=\{(0,0)\}$, which is closed.

import Mathlib

theorem la1_006_homogeneous_equation_closed (u v : ℝ × ℝ) (c : ℝ)
    (hu : u.1 + 2 * u.2 = 0) (hv : v.1 + 2 * v.2 = 0) :
    (u + v).1 + 2 * (u + v).2 = 0 ∧
      (c • u).1 + 2 * (c • u).2 = 0 := by
  constructor
  · simp only [Prod.fst_add, Prod.snd_add]
    linarith
  · simp only [Prod.smul_fst, Prod.smul_snd]
    linear_combination c * hu

problems.unit: Vector spaces, subspaces, sums, and direct sums
problems.title: The union of two axes is not a subspace
problems.objective: Disprove additive closure with a decisive pair of witnesses.
problems.statement: Let $H$ and $V$ be the horizontal and vertical axes in $\mathbb R^2$. Prove that $H\cup V$ is not a subspace by exhibiting two members whose sum is not in the union.
permittedResults: Failure of one subspace axiom is enough to disprove subspace status.
Membership in $H\cup V$ means at least one coordinate is zero.

hints: Choose one nonzero vector from each axis.
Check both coordinates of the sum against the union condition.
problems.solution: The vectors $(1,0)\in H$ and $(0,1)\in V$ both belong to $H\cup V$. Their sum is $(1,1)$, which lies on neither axis because neither coordinate is zero. Hence $H\cup V$ is not closed under addition and is not a subspace.
rubricCriteria: Chooses two vectors that really lie in the union.
Computes their sum correctly.
Shows the sum lies on neither axis and concludes failure of closure.

problems.leanDraft:
import Mathlib

theorem la1_008_standard_vectors_span (x y : ℝ) :
    ∃ a b : ℝ, (x, y) = a • (1, 0) + b • (0, 1) := by
  refine ⟨x, y, ?_⟩
  ext <;> simp

theorem la1_008_standard_coordinates_forced (x y a b : ℝ)
    (hrep : (x, y) = a • ((1, 0) : ℝ × ℝ) + b • ((0, 1) : ℝ × ℝ)) :
    a = x ∧ b = y := by
  have hx := congrArg (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => p.1) hrep
  have hy := congrArg (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => p.2) hrep
  norm_num at hx hy
  exact ⟨hx.symm, hy.symm⟩

problems.unit: Vector spaces, subspaces, sums, and direct sums
problems.title: Quadratics with zero constant term stay together
problems.objective: Track coefficients to verify a concrete polynomial subspace.
problems.statement: Let $P=\{p_{a,b}:p_{a,b}(x)=ax+bx^2,\ a,b\in\mathbb R\}$. Prove that the zero polynomial lies in $P$, and compute coefficients showing that $P$ is closed under addition and real scalar multiplication.

hints: Use $a=b=0$ for the zero polynomial.
Add $p_{a,b}(x)$ and $p_{c,d}(x)$ and group like powers.
Multiply by a scalar and read off the two new coefficients.
problems.solution: The choice $(a,b)=(0,0)$ gives the zero polynomial. Also $p_{a,b}+p_{c,d}=p_{a+c,b+d}$ because the coefficient of $x$ is $a+c$ and the coefficient of $x^2$ is $b+d$. For $r\in\mathbb R$, $rp_{a,b}=p_{ra,rb}$. Thus all three required closure properties hold.

Computes the coefficient pair for a sum.

problems.unit: Vector spaces, subspaces, sums, and direct sums
problems.title: Upper-triangular matrices pass the subspace test
problems.objective: Verify a matrix-defined subspace through its constrained entry.
problems.statement: Let $T$ be the set of real $2\times2$ upper-triangular matrices. Prove that the zero matrix belongs to $T$ and that, whenever $A,B\in T$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, both $A+B$ and $cA$ belong to $T$.
permittedResults: A $2\times2$ matrix is upper triangular exactly when its $(2,1)$ entry is zero.
Matrix addition and scalar multiplication are entrywise.
problems.strategy: First: Check the lower-left entry of the zero matrix. Next: Add the two lower-left entries of $A$ and $B$. Finally: Multiply the lower-left entry of $A$ by the arbitrary scalar $c$.
hints: Check the lower-left entry of the zero matrix.
Add the two lower-left entries of $A$ and $B$.
Multiply the lower-left entry of $A$ by the arbitrary scalar $c$.
problems.solution: The lower-left entry of the zero matrix is $0$. If $A_{21}=B_{21}=0$, then $(A+B)_{21}=A_{21}+B_{21}=0$. Also $(cA)_{21}=cA_{21}=c0=0$. Hence the zero matrix, every such sum, and every such scalar multiple are upper triangular.
rubricCriteria: Uses the lower-left entry to characterize membership.
Checks additive closure entrywise.
Checks scalar closure for an arbitrary real scalar.

commonErrors.description: Requires every entry below and above the diagonal to vanish.
commonErrors.consequence: Upper triangular matrices may have arbitrary entries on and above the diagonal; only the lower-left entry is constrained in size two.

commonErrors.description: Uses matrix multiplication instead of scalar multiplication.
commonErrors.consequence: The vector-subspace test concerns addition and multiplication by real scalars.

problems.flawedProof: Upper-triangular matrices have only diagonal entries. Adding two diagonal matrices or multiplying them together keeps that form, so $T$ is a vector subspace.

problems.unit: Vector spaces, subspaces, sums, and direct sums
problems.title: Distinct lines through the origin meet only at zero
problems.objective: Use two slope equations and a nonzero coefficient to determine an intersection.
problems.statement: For distinct real numbers $m\ne n$, let $L_m=\{(x,y):y=mx\}$ and $L_n=\{(x,y):y=nx\}$. Prove that $L_m\cap L_n=\{(0,0)\}$.
permittedResults: If $ab=0$ over $\mathbb R$, then $a=0$ or $b=0$.
The hypothesis $m\ne n$ implies $m-n\ne0$.
problems.strategy: First: A common point satisfies both $y=mx$ and $y=nx$. Next: Subtract the equations to obtain $(m-n)x=0$. Finally: Use $m\ne n$ to get $x=0$, then substitute for $y$.
hints: A common point satisfies both $y=mx$ and $y=nx$.
Subtract the equations to obtain $(m-n)x=0$.
Use $m\ne n$ to get $x=0$, then substitute for $y$.
problems.solution: If $(x,y)$ lies in both lines, then $mx=y=nx$, so $(m-n)x=0$. Since $m-n\ne0$, the zero-product property gives $x=0$, and then $y=mx=0$. Conversely the zero vector satisfies both equations.

Uses the distinct-slope hypothesis to force the first coordinate to zero.

commonErrors.consequence: Division is justified only because the slopes are distinct.

commonErrors.description: Proves the result only for two numerical slopes.
commonErrors.consequence: The claim is universal in distinct $m$ and $n$.

problems.flawedProof: From $(m-n)x=0$, divide by $m-n$ to obtain $x=0$. This division is always valid for real numbers, so the hypothesis $m\ne n$ is unnecessary.

import Mathlib

theorem la1_011_distinct_slope_intersection (m n x y : ℝ) (hmn : m ≠ n)
    (hm : y = m * x) (hn : y = n * x) : x = 0 ∧ y = 0 := by
  have hprod : (m - n) * x = 0 := by linarith
  have hcoef : m - n ≠ 0 := sub_ne_zero.mpr hmn
  have hx : x = 0 := (mul_eq_zero.mp hprod).resolve_left hcoef
  exact ⟨hx, by simp [hx] at hm ⊢; exact hm⟩

theorem la1_011_distinct_slope_intersection_iff
    (m n x y : ℝ) (hmn : m ≠ n) :
    (y = m * x ∧ y = n * x) ↔ x = 0 ∧ y = 0 := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨hm, hn⟩
    have hprod : (m - n) * x = 0 := by linarith
    have hcoef : m - n ≠ 0 := sub_ne_zero.mpr hmn
    have hx : x = 0 := (mul_eq_zero.mp hprod).resolve_left hcoef
    exact ⟨hx, by simp [hx] at hm ⊢; exact hm⟩
  · rintro ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
    simp

problems.statement:

  $$U+(V\cap W)\subseteq (U+V)\cap(U+W).$$
  Then show the reverse inclusion can fail in $\mathbb R^2$: take $U=\operatorname{span}(1,0)$, $V=\operatorname{span}(0,1)$, and $W=\operatorname{span}(1,1)$, and prove that $(0,1)$ belongs to the right-hand side but not the left-hand side.

problems.objective: Use two nested zero-intersection conditions to destroy a three-summand relation.
problems.statement: Let $U,V,W$ be subspaces of a vector space. Assume $U\cap(V+W)=\{0\}$ and $V\cap W=\{0\}$. Prove that whenever $u\in U$, $v\in V$, $w\in W$, and $u+v+w=0$, one has $u=v=w=0$.

Use the first intersection condition to obtain $u=0$ and reduce to $v+w=0$.
Now place $v=-w$ in $V\cap W$ and apply the second condition.

commonErrors.consequence: The relation gives $u=-(v+w)$, so membership follows only after taking the negative inside the subspace sum.

problems.objective: Connect linearity, idempotence, fixed vectors, kernel vectors, and unique decomposition.

Thus $r'=P(v)$ and then $k'=v-P(v)$, proving uniqueness.

commonErrors.consequence: Idempotence is $P(P(v))=P(v)$; vectors with nonzero third coordinate are not fixed.

problems.statement: Let $U,W$ be subspaces of an additive vector space and fix one decomposition $x=u_0+w_0$. Prove that every other decomposition $x=u+w$ is obtained in one and only one way as $u=u_0+t$, $w=w_0-t$ for a vector $t\in U\cap W$.

The formulas $u=u_0+t$ and $w=w_0-t$ follow. Conversely, any $t\in U\cap W$ gives valid summands and $(u_0+t)+(w_0-t)=x$. Uses the decomposition equality to place it in $W$ as well.

problems.title: An involution splits a space into fixed and sign-reversed parts
problems.objective: Construct complementary projections from an abstract linear symmetry.
problems.statement: Let $T:X\to X$ be a linear map on a real vector space with $T^2=I$. For each $x$, define $x_+=(x+Tx)/2$ and $x_-=(x-Tx)/2$. Prove $Tx_+=x_+$, $Tx_-=-x_-$, and $x=x_++x_-$. Prove this decomposition is unique among a fixed vector plus a sign-reversed vector, and deduce the two formulas define complementary idempotent projections.
permittedResults: Linearity gives $T(u\pm v)=Tu\pm Tv$.
The scalar $2$ is invertible over $\mathbb R$.
problems.strategy: First: Apply $T$ to both formulas and use $T(Tx)=x$. Next: For uniqueness, apply $T$ to $x=p+q$ and combine the resulting equations. Finally: Once the image of each formula has the required sign, applying its projection again is immediate.
hints: Apply $T$ to both formulas and use $T(Tx)=x$.
For uniqueness, apply $T$ to $x=p+q$ and combine the resulting equations.
Once the image of each formula has the required sign, applying its projection again is immediate.
problems.solution: Linearity and $T^2=I$ give $Tx_+=(Tx+x)/2=x_+$ and $Tx_-=(Tx-x)/2=-x_-$. Adding the formulas yields $x$. If $x=p+q$ with $Tp=p$ and $Tq=-q$, then $Tx=p-q$, so adding and subtracting the equations for $x$ and $Tx$ forces $p=(x+Tx)/2$ and $q=(x-Tx)/2$. Thus the decomposition is unique. Since $x_+$ is fixed and $x_-$ is sign-reversed, reapplying the corresponding formulas returns the same component, so both projections are idempotent and sum to $I$.

Derives the component formulas from an arbitrary competing decomposition.
Connects uniqueness and sign identities to complementary idempotence.

commonErrors.description: Assumes a fixed vector and a sign-reversed vector cannot overlap without proof.
commonErrors.consequence: Uniqueness must be derived by applying $T$ and solving the two equations.

problems.title: The always-valid intersection inclusion can be strict
problems.objective: Prove the safe distributive inclusion and construct a sharp failure of equality.
problems.statement: For subspaces $U,V,W$, prove $(U\cap V)+(U\cap W)\subseteq U\cap(V+W)$. Then in $\mathbb R^2$ take $U$ as the $x$-axis, $V=\operatorname{span}(1,1)$, and $W=\operatorname{span}(1,-1)$; compute the relevant intersections and use $(1,0)$ to prove the inclusion is strict.

problems.title: A nested-intersection criterion forces a three-way direct sum
problems.objective: Derive uniqueness of three summands from the correct two-stage intersection conditions.
problems.statement: Let $U,V,W$ be subspaces. Assume $U\cap V=\{0\}$ and $(U+V)\cap W=\{0\}$. Prove that whenever $u_1+v_1+w_1=u_2+v_2+w_2$ with $u_i\in U$, $v_i\in V$, and $w_i\in W$, the three corresponding pairs of summands are equal.

theorem la1_037_three_summand_uniqueness
    {X : Type*} [AddCommGroup X] (U V W : X → Prop)
    (Usub : ∀ a b, U a → U b → U (a - b))
    (Vsub : ∀ a b, V a → V b → V (a - b))
    (Wsub : ∀ a b, W a → W b → W (a - b))
    (hUV : ∀ z, U z → V z → z = 0)
    (hUVW : ∀ z, (∃ u v, U u ∧ V v ∧ z = u + v) → W z → z = 0) :
    ∀ u₁ u₂ v₁ v₂ w₁ w₂,
      U u₁ → U u₂ → V v₁ → V v₂ → W w₁ → W w₂ →
      u₁ + v₁ + w₁ = u₂ + v₂ + w₂ →
        u₁ = u₂ ∧ v₁ = v₂ ∧ w₁ = w₂ := by
  intro u₁ u₂ v₁ v₂ w₁ w₂ hu₁ hu₂ hv₁ hv₂ hw₁ hw₂ heq
  have hside : (u₁ - u₂) + (v₁ - v₂) = w₂ - w₁ := by
    calc
      (u₁ - u₂) + (v₁ - v₂) =
          (u₁ + v₁ + w₁) - (u₂ + v₂ + w₁) := by abel
      _ = (u₂ + v₂ + w₂) - (u₂ + v₂ + w₁) := by rw [heq]
      _ = w₂ - w₁ := by abel
  have hz : (u₁ - u₂) + (v₁ - v₂) = 0 :=
    hUVW ((u₁ - u₂) + (v₁ - v₂))
      ⟨u₁ - u₂, v₁ - v₂, Usub u₁ u₂ hu₁ hu₂,
        Vsub v₁ v₂ hv₁ hv₂, rfl⟩
      (hside ▸ Wsub w₂ w₁ hw₂ hw₁)
  have hdiff : u₁ - u₂ = v₂ - v₁ := by
    calc
      u₁ - u₂ = -(v₁ - v₂) := eq_neg_of_add_eq_zero_left hz
      _ = v₂ - v₁ := by abel
  have hu : u₁ - u₂ = 0 :=
    hUV (u₁ - u₂) (Usub u₁ u₂ hu₁ hu₂)
      (hdiff ▸ Vsub v₂ v₁ hv₂ hv₁)
  have huv : u₁ = u₂ := sub_eq_zero.mp hu
  have hv : v₁ = v₂ := by
    apply sub_eq_zero.mp
    rw [huv] at hz
    simpa using hz
  have hw : w₁ = w₂ := by
    rw [huv, hv] at heq
    exact add_left_cancel heq

In any such decomposition, the second coordinate forces the graph parameter to be $w$, and the first then forces the horizontal part to be $u-Aw$, proving uniqueness. Conversely, fix a complement $C$. Decomposing $(0,w)$ shows that some $(u,w)$ lies in $C$. problems.objective: Characterize complement generators, normalize them, and exhibit infinitely many distinct complements.
problems.statement: Let $Z=\{f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R:f(0)=0\}$. Prove $Z$ and $\operatorname{span}\{g\}$ uniquely decompose every function if and only if $g(0)\ne0$. Derive $c=f(0)/g(0)$ and $z=f-cg$; when $g(0)=0$, use the constant function $1$ as an obstruction. If $g(0),h(0)\ne0$, prove $\exists t\,\forall x,\ g(x)=t h(x)$ if and only if $g(x)/g(0)=h(x)/h(0)$ for every $x$. Prove $g_m(x)=1+mx$ gives distinct complements for distinct $m$.

problems.statement: Let $T:C\to X$ be surjective and linear. Prove $T$ is injective if and only if every $x\in X$ has exactly one preimage. Let $S:X\to C$ be a linear right inverse. Prove every $c\in C$ has the unique decomposition $c=(c-S(Tc))+S(Tc)$ with the first term in $\ker T$ and the second in $\operatorname{range}S$.   · intro L hL
    apply LinearEquiv.ext
    intro x
    have hmaps : L.toLinearMap = (b.equiv c e).toLinearMap := by
      apply b.ext
      intro i
      simpa [Module.Basis.equiv] using hL.1 i
    exact LinearMap.congr_fun hmaps x
